patient_information: A 7-year-old girl who lives in the Peruvian capital, Lima. The girl is otherwise healthy.
chief_complaint: A chronic skin lesion on her nose, present for 4 months.
history_of_present_illness: The patient was brought to a local clinic for a chronic skin lesion on her nose. The lesion appeared 4 months ago as a small nodule and slowly turned into an ulcer. It is reported to be a bit itchy but not painful. There is no history of trauma, and the girl is otherwise healthy.
exposure_and_epidemiology: The patient lives in Lima, Peru. Six months ago, she travelled to a valley on the western slopes of the Andes, which is an endemic area for leishmaniasis.
physical_exam: The lesion is a localized ulcer on the nose, about 2cm in diameter. The borders of the ulcer are indurated, and there is a plaque-like infiltration of the surrounding skin. There are no palpable lymph nodes. The rest of the physical examination is normal. After the scab was removed, the ulcer revealed a cobblestone-patterned bottom and raised edges, typical of cutaneous leishmaniasis.
labs_and_diagnostics: The microscopic examination of a sample obtained by scraping under the edges of the lesion was negative. The Montenegro or leishmanin skin test was positive. Polymerase chain reaction (PCR) was also positive, and the infecting species was identified as Leishmania (Viannia) peruviana.
differential_diagnosis: The differential diagnoses included infectious diseases such as cutaneous leishmaniasis, sporotrichosis, cutaneous tuberculosis, and infection by Balamuthia mandrillaris. Common bacterial infections were less likely given the chronic nature of the lesion. Cutaneous leishmaniasis was considered the most likely diagnosis due to the frequency of the disease in the valley the patient had travelled to and the characteristic presentation of a localized, painless ulcer with raised edges. Sporotrichosis was considered as it is hyperendemic in parts of the Peruvian Andes, but the patient did not travel to such a place. Cutaneous tuberculosis was also considered, as the patient lives in a poor neighbourhood with a high incidence of tuberculosis.
management_and_clinical_course: A definitive diagnosis of cutaneous leishmaniasis was made. Treatment was started with intravenous sodium stibogluconate (SSG, 20mg/kg/day for 20 days), which is the first-line treatment for L. (V.) peruviana in Peru. In addition, the girl received topical imiquimod therapy, administered every other day for 20 days. The response after 20 days of treatment was good. At the third month of follow-up, the patient did not have any signs of relapse.
final_diagnosis: The final diagnosis was cutaneous leishmaniasis caused by Leishmania (Viannia) peruviana. This was based on the patient's presentation with a chronic, 4-month-old, painless ulcer on the nose with indurated, raised borders and a cobblestone-patterned bottom. The patient had a history of travel six months prior to a valley on the western slopes of the Andes, an endemic area for the disease. Although microscopic examination of a scraping was negative, the diagnosis was confirmed by a positive leishmanin skin test and a positive PCR, which identified the causative species. The lesion responded well to treatment with sodium stibogluconate and topical imiquimod.
